claim: Wnt3a and Wnt5a dramatically reduced the expression of FZD5 and FZD8 on the cell surface without significantly affecting other FZD receptors in HEK293A cells.
source: Both Wnt3a and Wnt5a dramatically reduced the expression of FZD5 and FZD8 on the cell surface without significantly affecting other FZD receptors (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating specific reduction of FZD5/8 surface levels upon Wnt treatment.

claim: Both Wnt3a and Wnt5a reduced the mature protein levels of both FZD5 and FZD8.
source: Immunoblotting revealed that both Wnt3a and Wnt5a reduced the mature protein levels of both FZD5 and FZD8 (the upper bands of FZD5 and FZD8) (Figure 1B; Chen et al., 2020; Koo et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1B showing reduction of mature FZD5/8 bands, with citations to previous work characterizing FZD maturation.

claim: Treatment with the lysosomal inhibitor bafilomycin A1 rescued the mature form of FZD5 that was reduced by Wnt3a and Wnt5a.
source: Treatment with the lysosomal inhibitor bafilomycin A1 rescued the mature form of FZD5 that was reduced by Wnt3a and Wnt5a (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1C showing restoration of FZD5 levels with bafilomycin A1 treatment.

claim: Both Wnt3a and Wnt5a specifically reduced FZD5 and FZD8 on the cell surface in Huh7 cells.
source: Huh7 cells stably expressing each of ten V5-FZDs were also treated with control, Wnt3a, or Wnt5a CM, and both Wnt3a and Wnt5a specifically reduced FZD5 and FZD8 on the cell surface (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing specific reduction in Huh7 cells.

claim: Only the mature form of FZD5 showed decreased levels upon Wnt3a or Wnt5a treatment in U2OS cells.
source: U2OS cells stably expressing V5-FZD1/FZD4/FZD5/FZD7 were treated with control, Wnt3a, Wnt5a CM, and only the mature form of FZD5 showed decreased levels upon Wnt3a or Wnt5a treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D showing selective FZD5 reduction in U2OS cells.

claim: Wnt3a and Wnt5a specifically promote the endocytosis and lysosomal degradation of FZD5 and FZD8.
source: These results suggest that Wnt3a and Wnt5a specifically promote the endocytosis and lysosomal degradation of FZD5 and FZD8.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing Wnt-induced reduction of surface FZD5/8, reduction of mature protein, and rescue by lysosomal inhibitor.

claim: The CRD domain, but not the C-terminal tail, is crucial for Wnt3a/Wnt5a-induced FZD5 endocytosis.
source: The results indicated that the CRD domain, but not the C-terminal tail, is crucial for Wnt3a/Wnt5a-induced FZD5 endocytosis (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1D-F showing that FZD5ΔCRD but not FZD5ΔC abolishes Wnt-induced endocytosis.

claim: Wnt3a or Wnt5a treatment reduced the cell surface levels of FZD5CRD-FZD4 and FZD5CRD-FZD7 but had little effect on the cell surface levels of FZD4CRD-FZD5 or FZD7CRD-FZD5.
source: Wnt3a or Wnt5a treatment reduced the cell surface levels of FZD5CRD-FZD4 and FZD5CRD-FZD7 but had little effect on the cell surface levels of FZD4CRD-FZD5 or FZD7CRD-FZD5 (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1H showing that FZD5 CRD domain is sufficient to confer Wnt-induced endocytosis.

claim: Wnt-induced FZD5/8-specific endocytosis relies on their CRD domains.
source: These results suggest that Wnt-induced FZD5/8-specific endocytosis relies on their CRD domains.
evidence: Inferred from domain deletion and domain swap experiments showing CRD requirement.

claim: Both Wnt3a and Wnt5a treatments reduced the intensity of the upper band representing the mature form of endogenous FZD5 as early as one hour after treatment in FZD5 knock-in HEK293A cells.
source: Like V5-FZD5 overexpression, the endogenous FZD5-V5 protein exhibited two major bands on immunoblotting, and both the Wnt3a and Wnt5a treatments reduced the intensity of the upper band representing the mature form of FZD5, which occurred as early as one hour after treatment (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2A showing time-dependent reduction of endogenous FZD5.

claim: Neither Wnt3a nor Wnt5a induced degradation of endogenous FZD7 in FZD7-V5 knock-in cells.
source: Using the same approach, we generated a FZD7-V5 knock-in cell line and observed that neither Wnt3a nor Wnt5a induced degradation of endogenous FZD7 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2B showing no change in FZD7 levels with Wnt treatment.

claim: Treatment with the Porcupine inhibitor IWP-2 increased the level of the endogenous mature FZD5 protein but did not affect FZD7 levels.
source: Furthermore, treatment with the Porcupine inhibitor IWP-2 increased the level of the endogenous mature FZD5 protein but did not affect FZD7 levels (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2C showing selective increase in FZD5 with IWP-2.

claim: IWP-2 treatment increased the cell surface levels of FZD5/8 but had little effect on FZD4 levels in HEK293A cells.
source: Flow cytometry with anti-FZD5/8 or anti-FZD4 monoclonal antibodies revealed that IWP-2 treatment increased the cell surface levels of FZD5/8 but had little effect on FZD4 levels in HEK293A cells (Figure 2D and E; Pan et al., 2021; Sachdev Sidhu et al., 2021; Steinhart et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2D and E, with citations to antibody characterization studies.

claim: IWP-2 treatment increased the cell surface levels of FZD5/8 in Huh7, MCF7, and 769P cells.
source: IWP-2 treatment also increased the cell surface levels of FZD5/8 in Huh7, MCF7, and 769 P cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C showing consistent effects across cell lines.

claim: Wnt specifically induces the endocytosis and degradation of endogenous FZD5/8.
source: These results further indicate that Wnt specifically induces the endocytosis and degradation of endogenous FZD5/8.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments with endogenous FZD5/8 showing Wnt-induced reduction and IWP-2-induced increase.

claim: ZNRF3/RNF43 double knockout increased FZD5/8 levels on the cell surface.
source: Flow cytometry analysis with an anti-FZD5/8 antibody revealed that ZNRF3/RNF43 double knockout increased FZD5/8 levels on the cell surface (Figure 2F), which is consistent with previous reports (Hao et al., 2012; Koo et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2F, with citations to previous studies showing similar findings.

claim: The membrane levels of FZD4 remained unchanged in ZRDKO cells.
source: In contrast, the membrane levels of FZD4 remained unchanged in ZRDKO cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2G showing no change in FZD4 levels.

claim: Neither Wnt3a nor Wnt5a induced the degradation of endogenous mature FZD5 in ZRDKO cells.
source: Immunoblotting revealed that neither Wnt3a nor Wnt5a induced the degradation of endogenous mature FZD5 in ZRDKO cells (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2H showing no FZD5 reduction in ZRDKO cells.

claim: IWP-2 treatment did not further increase mature FZD5 levels in ZRDKO cells.
source: Additionally, IWP-2 treatment did not further increase mature FZD5 levels in ZRDKO cells (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2I showing no additional increase with IWP-2 in ZRDKO cells.

claim: RSPO1 significantly increased the level of endogenous mature FZD5 but did not affect the FZD7 level.
source: Immunoblotting revealed that RSPO1 significantly increased the level of endogenous mature FZD5 but did not affect the FZD7 level (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2J showing selective FZD5 increase with RSPO1.

claim: RSPO1 had little effect on FZD5 levels in ZRDKO cells.
source: Moreover, RSPO1 had little effect on FZD5 levels in ZRDKO cells (Figure 2K).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2K showing no FZD5 increase with RSPO1 in ZRDKO cells.

claim: Wnt3a and Wnt5a induced membrane FZD5 degradation, which was blocked by cotreatment with RSPO1.
source: Results showed that Wnt3a and Wnt5a induced membrane FZD5 degradation, which was blocked by cotreatment with RSPO1 (Figure 2L).
evidence: Supported by surface biotinylation assay data in Figure 2L showing RSPO1 blocks Wnt-induced FZD5 degradation.

claim: Both IWP-2 and RSPO1 treatments similarly elevated FZD5/8 levels on the cell surface in wild-type HEK293A cells.
source: Flow cytometry analysis of wild-type (WT) HEK293A cells treated with IWP-2 or RSPO1 revealed that both treatments similarly elevated FZD5/8 levels on the cell surface (Figure 2M).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2M showing comparable effects of IWP-2 and RSPO1.

claim: RSPO1 treatment did not increase membrane FZD5/8 levels in ZRDKO cells or FZD4 levels in WT cells.
source: However, RSPO1 treatment did not increase membrane FZD5/8 levels in ZRDKO cells or FZD4 levels in WT cells (Figure 2N and O).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2N and O showing no effect of RSPO1 in these conditions.

claim: ZNRF3/RNF43 specifically degrades FZD5/8 under Wnt stimulation, which is antagonized by RSPO.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that ZNRF3/RNF43 specifically degrades FZD5/8 under Wnt stimulation, which is antagonized by RSPO.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing ZNRF3/RNF43-dependent Wnt-induced FZD5/8 degradation and RSPO rescue.

claim: Triple knockout of DVL1/2/3 increased the cell surface levels of FZD5/8.
source: Flow cytometry analysis revealed that triple knockout of DVL1/2/3 increased the cell surface levels of FZD5/8 (Figure 3B), suggesting that DVL proteins promote FZD5/8 endocytosis, which is consistent with a previous report (Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3B, with citation to previous work on DVL function.

claim: Both IWP-2 and RSPO1 treatments further elevated the cell surface levels of FZD5/8 in DVLTKO cells.
source: However, both IWP-2 and RSPO1 treatments further elevated the cell surface levels of FZD5/8 in DVLTKO cells (Figure 3C and D), indicating that Wnt can still induce ZNRF3/RNF43-dependent FZD5/8 endocytosis even in the absence of DVL proteins.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3C and D showing additional increase with IWP-2/RSPO1 in DVLTKO cells.

claim: Wnt3a and Wnt5a reduced both the cell surface level and the mature form of the FZD5 protein in DVLTKO cells stably expressing V5-FZD5.
source: Furthermore, Wnt3a and Wnt5a reduced both the cell surface level and the mature form of the FZD5 protein in DVLTKO cells stably expressing V5-FZD5, as assessed by flow cytometry and immunoblotting (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and immunoblotting data in Figure 3E and F showing Wnt-induced FZD5 reduction in DVLTKO cells.

claim: DVLTKO cells presented fewer FZD5 puncta in the control CM-treated group compared with WT cells, and re-expressing DVL2 in DVLTKO cells elevated FZD5 puncta.
source: Compared with WT cells, DVLTKO cells presented fewer FZD5 puncta in the control CM-treated group, and re-expressing DVL2 in DVLTKO cells elevated FZD5 puncta, whereas Wnt3a and Wnt5a increased the number of FZD5 puncta in both WT, DVLTKO, and DVLTKO + DVL2 cells, as quantified by the number of FZD5 puncta (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification in Figure 3G and 3H showing differential FZD5 endocytosis.

claim: Wnt3a and Wnt5a increased the number of FZD5 puncta in both WT, DVLTKO, and DVLTKO + DVL2 cells.
source: Compared with WT cells, DVLTKO cells presented fewer FZD5 puncta in the control CM-treated group, and re-expressing DVL2 in DVLTKO cells elevated FZD5 puncta, whereas Wnt3a and Wnt5a increased the number of FZD5 puncta in both WT, DVLTKO, and DVLTKO + DVL2 cells, as quantified by the number of FZD5 puncta (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification in Figure 3G and 3H showing Wnt-induced FZD5 endocytosis independent of DVL.

claim: DVLTKO cells presented decreased FZD7 internalization in control CM, which could be rescued by re-expressing DVL2, and Wnt3a or Wnt5a CM had no effect on FZD7 endocytosis in either WT, DVLTKO, or DVLTKO + DVL2 cells.
source: Compared with WT cells, DVLTKO cells presented decreased FZD7 internalization in control CM, which could also be rescued by re-expressing DVL2, and Wnt3a or Wnt5a CM had no effect on FZD7 endocytosis in either WT, DVLTKO, or DVLTKO + DVL2 cells (Figure 3I and J).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification in Figure 3I and 3J showing DVL-dependent but Wnt-independent FZD7 endocytosis.

claim: DVL proteins participate in Wnt-independent FZD receptor endocytosis but are dispensable for Wnt-induced FZD5/8 endocytosis and degradation.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that DVL proteins participate in Wnt-independent FZD receptor endocytosis but are dispensable for Wnt-induced FZD5/8 endocytosis and degradation.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing DVL-dependent basal endocytosis but DVL-independent Wnt-induced FZD5/8 degradation.

claim: Wnt3a or Wnt5a CM treatment reduced the cell surface level of V5-FZD5 in ZRDKO cells.
source: We found that Wnt3a or Wnt5a CM treatment reduced the cell surface level of V5-FZD5 in ZRDKO cells, as determined by flow cytometry (Figure 4A), although they had little effect on the total protein level of FZD5 (Figure 4B), suggesting that Wnt induces FZD5 internalization independent of ZNRF3/RNF43.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4A showing surface reduction despite no total protein change.

claim: Wnt3a and Wnt5a had little effect on the total protein level of FZD5 in ZRDKO cells.
source: We found that Wnt3a or Wnt5a CM treatment reduced the cell surface level of V5-FZD5 in ZRDKO cells, as determined by flow cytometry (Figure 4A), although they had little effect on the total protein level of FZD5 (Figure 4B), suggesting that Wnt induces FZD5 internalization independent of ZNRF3/RNF43.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 4B showing no change in total FZD5 protein.

claim: Wnt induces FZD5 internalization independent of ZNRF3/RNF43.
source: We found that Wnt3a or Wnt5a CM treatment reduced the cell surface level of V5-FZD5 in ZRDKO cells, as determined by flow cytometry (Figure 4A), although they had little effect on the total protein level of FZD5 (Figure 4B), suggesting that Wnt induces FZD5 internalization independent of ZNRF3/RNF43.
evidence: Inferred from data showing Wnt-induced surface reduction without total protein change in ZNRF3/RNF43 knockout cells.

claim: A significant amount of FZD5 was internalized into the intracellular vesicles in both WT and ZRDKO cells after Wnt3a and Wnt5a treatment for one hour, and the FZD5 signals gradually diminished in WT but not ZRDKO cells after Wnt3a and Wnt5a treatment for two and four hours.
source: The results revealed that a significant amount of FZD5 was internalized into the intracellular vesicles in both WT and ZRDKO cells after Wnt3a and Wnt5a treatment for one hour, and the FZD5 signals gradually diminished in WT but not ZRDKO cells after Wnt3a and Wnt5a treatment for two and four hours (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), indicating that ZNRF3/RNF43 is required for the degradation of internalized FZD5 but not for Wnt-induced FZD5 internalization.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence time-course data in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A showing differential FZD5 fate in WT vs ZRDKO cells.

claim: ZNRF3/RNF43 is required for the degradation of internalized FZD5 but not for Wnt-induced FZD5 internalization.
source: The results revealed that a significant amount of FZD5 was internalized into the intracellular vesicles in both WT and ZRDKO cells after Wnt3a and Wnt5a treatment for one hour, and the FZD5 signals gradually diminished in WT but not ZRDKO cells after Wnt3a and Wnt5a treatment for two and four hours (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), indicating that ZNRF3/RNF43 is required for the degradation of internalized FZD5 but not for Wnt-induced FZD5 internalization.
evidence: Inferred from time-course data showing internalization in both cell types but degradation only in WT cells.

claim: Cotreatment with RSPO1 prevented FZD5 degradation but had little effect on FZD5 internalization induced by Wnt3a and Wnt5a.
source: Furthermore, cotreatment with RSPO1 prevented FZD5 degradation but had little effect on FZD5 internalization induced by Wnt3a and Wnt5a (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B showing RSPO1 blocks degradation but not internalization.

claim: Under Wnt5a treatment, internalized FZD5 colocalized with either EEA1, an early endosomal marker, or LAMP1, a lysosomal marker, in WT cells, whereas this colocalization was significantly reduced in ZRDKO cells.
source: Under Wnt5a treatment, internalized FZD5 colocalized with either EEA1, an early endosomal marker, or LAMP1, a lysosomal marker, in WT cells, whereas this colocalization was significantly reduced in ZRDKO cells (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: Supported by colocalization immunofluorescence data and quantification in Figure 4E-H showing differential endosomal/lysosomal trafficking.

claim: ZNRF3/RNF43 promotes endolysosomal transport and degradation of internalized FZD5, whereas in ZRDKO cells, internalized FZD5 may be recycled back to the plasma membrane for reuse.
source: These results suggest that ZNRF3/RNF43 promotes endolysosomal transport and degradation of internalized FZD5, whereas in ZRDKO cells, internalized FZD5 may be recycled back to the plasma membrane for reuse.
evidence: Inferred from data showing reduced endosomal/lysosomal colocalization and accumulation of internalized FZD5 in ZRDKO cells.

claim: HEK293A cells stably expressing V5-FZD5 or V5-FZD7 presented significantly higher FZD protein levels on the cell surface than ZRDKO cells did.
source: Although HEK293A cells stably expressing V5-FZD5 or V5-FZD7 presented significantly higher FZD protein levels on the cell surface than ZRDKO cells did, as measured by flow cytometry with an anti-pan-FZD antibody (Figure 5A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), these cells presented markedly lower cytosolic β-catenin levels than ZRDKO cells did (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5A showing higher surface FZD in overexpressing cells.

claim: HEK293A cells stably expressing V5-FZD5 or V5-FZD7 presented markedly lower cytosolic β-catenin levels than ZRDKO cells did.
source: Although HEK293A cells stably expressing V5-FZD5 or V5-FZD7 presented significantly higher FZD protein levels on the cell surface than ZRDKO cells did, as measured by flow cytometry with an anti-pan-FZD antibody (Figure 5A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), these cells presented markedly lower cytosolic β-catenin levels than ZRDKO cells did (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 5B showing lower β-catenin in FZD-overexpressing cells.

claim: The increase in DVL proteins phosphorylation and cytosolic β-catenin observed in ZNRF3/RNF43 double knockout cells could be reversed by IWP-2 treatment.
source: The increase in DVL proteins phosphorylation and cytosolic β-catenin observed in ZNRF3/RNF43 double knockout cells could be reversed by IWP-2 treatment, whereas IWP-2 had a minimal effect on DVL phosphorylation in cells overexpressing V5-FZD5 or V5-FZD7 (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 5C showing IWP-2 reverses signaling in ZRDKO cells.

claim: IWP-2 had a minimal effect on DVL phosphorylation in cells overexpressing V5-FZD5 or V5-FZD7.
source: The increase in DVL proteins phosphorylation and cytosolic β-catenin observed in ZNRF3/RNF43 double knockout cells could be reversed by IWP-2 treatment, whereas IWP-2 had a minimal effect on DVL phosphorylation in cells overexpressing V5-FZD5 or V5-FZD7 (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 5D showing minimal IWP-2 effect in FZD-overexpressing cells.

claim: Elevated Wnt signaling in ZRDKO cells cannot be solely attributed to increased FZD protein levels on the cell surface.
source: These findings suggest that elevated Wnt signaling in ZRDKO cells cannot be solely attributed to increased FZD protein levels on the cell surface.
evidence: Inferred from comparison showing ZRDKO cells have higher signaling despite lower surface FZD than overexpressing cells.

claim: Only ZNRF3 or RNF43 decreased the cytosolic β-catenin levels in ZRDKO cells, while RNF130 and RNF150 did not.
source: Furthermore, RNF130 and RNF150 are two structurally similar transmembrane E3 ubiquitin ligases compared to ZNRF3 and RNF43. These four E3 ubiquitin ligases were overexpressed into ZRDKO cells, and only ZNRF3 or RNF43 decreased the cytosolic β-catenin levels in ZRDKO cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 5E showing selective effect of ZNRF3/RNF43 on β-catenin.

claim: Expressing RNF43 or RNF150 in HEK293A cells stably expressing V5-FZD5 or V5-FZD7 efficiently decreased the levels of the mature forms of FZD5 and FZD7.
source: However, expressing RNF43 or RNF150 in HEK293A cells stably expressing V5-FZD5 or V5-FZD7 efficiently decreased the levels of the mature forms of FZD5 and FZD7 (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 5F showing both E3 ligases reduce FZD levels.

claim: Each of the four E3 ligases (ZNRF3, RNF43, RNF130, RNF150) reduced FZD protein levels on the cell surface of the ZRDKO cells to a comparable degree.
source: Each of these E3 ligases reduced FZD protein levels on the cell surface of the ZRDKO cells to a comparable degree, as determined by flow cytometry with an anti-pan-FZD antibody (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5G showing similar surface FZD reduction by all four E3 ligases.

claim: Each of the four E3 ligases reduced FZD5/8 levels on the cell surface in ZRDKO cells, with IWP-2 partially restoring the effects of ZNRF3 and RNF43 but not those of RNF130 or RNF150.
source: Furthermore, each of the four E3 ligases also reduced FZD5/8 levels on the cell surface in ZRDKO cells, with IWP-2 partially restoring the effects of ZNRF3 and RNF43 but not those of RNF130 or RNF150 (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5H showing differential IWP-2 sensitivity.

claim: Overexpressing a transmembrane E3 ubiquitin ligase may nonspecifically degrade FZD receptors and the specific ability of ZNRF3 and RNF43 to degrade FZD is dependent on Wnt ligands.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that overexpressing a transmembrane E3 ubiquitin ligase may nonspecifically degrade FZD receptors and that the specific ability of ZNRF3 and RNF43 to degrade FZD is dependent on Wnt ligands.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing all E3 ligases reduce FZD when overexpressed, but only ZNRF3/RNF43 show Wnt-dependent effects.

claim: The depletion of FZD5/8 in ZRDKO cells dramatically reduced cytosolic β-catenin levels.
source: Immunoblotting revealed that the depletion of FZD5/8 in ZRDKO cells dramatically reduced cytosolic β-catenin levels (Figure 6B), which were restored by re-expressing FZD5 but not FZD7 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 6B showing reduced β-catenin in ZRDKO-FZD5/8DKO cells.

claim: Cytosolic β-catenin levels in ZRDKO-FZD5/8DKO cells were restored by re-expressing FZD5 but not FZD7.
source: Immunoblotting revealed that the depletion of FZD5/8 in ZRDKO cells dramatically reduced cytosolic β-catenin levels (Figure 6B), which were restored by re-expressing FZD5 but not FZD7 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 6C showing selective rescue by FZD5.

claim: Stably expressing FZD5 but not FZD7 further elevated cytosolic β-catenin levels in ZRDKO cells.
source: Furthermore, stably expressing FZD5 but not FZD7 further elevated cytosolic β-catenin levels in ZRDKO cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 6D showing selective effect of FZD5 overexpression.

claim: Coexpressing FZD5 but not FZD7 in RNF43-expressing cells increased the inhibitory effect of RNF43 on Wnt3a-induced β-catenin accumulation in HEK293A cells.
source: Additionally, stable expression of RNF43 in HEK293A or U2OS cells had a minimal effect on Wnt3a-induced β-catenin accumulation; interestingly, coexpressing FZD5 but not FZD7 in RNF43-expressing cells increased the inhibitory effect of RNF43 on Wnt3a-induced β-catenin accumulation (Figure 6E and F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 6E and F showing FZD5-specific enhancement of RNF43 inhibition.

claim: Coexpressing FZD5 but not FZD7 in RNF43-expressing cells increased the inhibitory effect of RNF43 on Wnt3a-induced β-catenin accumulation in U2OS cells.
source: Additionally, stable expression of RNF43 in HEK293A or U2OS cells had a minimal effect on Wnt3a-induced β-catenin accumulation; interestingly, coexpressing FZD5 but not FZD7 in RNF43-expressing cells increased the inhibitory effect of RNF43 on Wnt3a-induced β-catenin accumulation (Figure 6E and F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B showing similar effects in U2OS cells.

claim: FZD5/8 double knockout had little effect on Wnt3a-induced cytosolic β-catenin accumulation but dramatically abolished RSPO1-induced cytosolic β-catenin accumulation.
source: Immunoblotting revealed that FZD5/8 double knockout had little effect on Wnt3a-induced cytosolic β-catenin accumulation but dramatically abolished RSPO1-induced cytosolic β-catenin accumulation (Figure 6H and I), which was reversed by re-expressing FZD5 or FZD8 in FZD5/8 DKO cells (Figure 6J and K).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 6H and I showing differential effects on Wnt3a vs RSPO1 signaling.

claim: RSPO1-induced cytosolic β-catenin accumulation was reversed by re-expressing FZD5 or FZD8 in FZD5/8 DKO cells.
source: Immunoblotting revealed that FZD5/8 double knockout had little effect on Wnt3a-induced cytosolic β-catenin accumulation but dramatically abolished RSPO1-induced cytosolic β-catenin accumulation (Figure 6H and I), which was reversed by re-expressing FZD5 or FZD8 in FZD5/8 DKO cells (Figure 6J and K).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 6J and K showing rescue of RSPO1 signaling by FZD5/8 re-expression.

claim: RSPO1 enhances Wnt signaling primarily through FZD5/8, whereas ZNRF3/RNF43 specifically inhibits Wnt signaling mediated by FZD5/8.
source: Collectively, these findings indicate that RSPO1 enhances Wnt signaling primarily through FZD5/8, whereas ZNRF3/RNF43 specifically inhibits Wnt signaling mediated by FZD5/8.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing FZD5/8-specific effects of RSPO1 and ZNRF3/RNF43 on Wnt signaling.

claim: Both Wnt3a and Wnt5a significantly increased the biotinylation of RNF43ΔRING in FZD5-mTB-expressing cells but not in FZD7-mTB-expressing cells.
source: Both Wnt3a and Wnt5a significantly increased the biotinylation of RNF43ΔRING in FZD5-mTB-expressing cells but not in FZD7-mTB-expressing cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by proximity labeling data in Figure 7B showing Wnt-induced FZD5-RNF43 interaction.

claim: IWP-2 treatment reduced the basal biotinylation of RNF43ΔRING in FZD5-mTB-expressing cells.
source: Additionally, IWP-2 treatment reduced the basal biotinylation of RNF43ΔRING in FZD5-mTB-expressing cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by proximity labeling data in Figure 7B showing reduced basal interaction with IWP-2.

claim: DVL proteins did not participate in Wnt3a or Wnt5a-induced FZD5 and RNF43 interaction.
source: We further replicated the biotin-based proximity labeling assay in DVLTKO cells. The results showed that DVL proteins did not participate in Wnt3a or Wnt5a-induced FZD5 and RNF43 interaction (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by proximity labeling data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B showing Wnt-induced interaction in DVLTKO cells.

claim: Wnt specifically induces DVL proteins independent of interaction between FZD5 and RNF43 at the plasma membrane.
source: These results suggest that Wnt specifically induces DVL proteins independent of interaction between FZD5 and RNF43 at the plasma membrane.
evidence: Inferred from proximity labeling data showing Wnt-induced FZD5-RNF43 interaction occurs in the absence of DVL.

claim: Wnt signaling employs a strategy analogous to that of receptor–tyrosine kinase pathways, where ligands bind to and activate receptors while simultaneously inducing receptor endocytosis and degradation to modulate signaling strength and duration.
source: Our results demonstrate that Wnt signaling employs a strategy analogous to that of receptor–tyrosine kinase pathways, where ligands bind to and activate receptors while simultaneously inducing receptor endocytosis and degradation to modulate signaling strength and duration (Alexander, 1998; Sorkin and Waters, 1993).
evidence: Inferred from the study's findings with citations to established mechanisms in RTK pathways.

claim: In the presence of ZNRF3/RNF43, Wnt binds to FZD5/8, forming a complex with ZNRF3/RNF43 and facilitating FZD5/8 endocytosis and subsequent lysosomal degradation, and this process occurs independently of DVL proteins.
source: In the presence of ZNRF3/RNF43, Wnt binds to FZD5/8, forming a complex with ZNRF3/RNF43 and facilitating FZD5/8 endocytosis and subsequent lysosomal degradation, and this process occurs independently of DVL proteins.
evidence: Summary statement integrating multiple findings from the study.

claim: In the absence of ZNRF3/RNF43, Wnt still induces FZD5/8 endocytosis; however, endosomes harboring FZD5/8 fail to merge with lysosomes, leading to the accumulation of mature FZD5/8 within the cell, which may be recycled back to the plasma membrane for reuse to sustain signaling activity.
source: In the absence of ZNRF3/RNF43, Wnt still induces FZD5/8 endocytosis; however, endosomes harboring FZD5/8 fail to merge with lysosomes, leading to the accumulation of mature FZD5/8 within the cell, which may be recycled back to the plasma membrane for reuse to sustain signaling activity (Figure 7C).
evidence: Summary statement integrating multiple findings with reference to model figure, includes speculative element about recycling.

claim: FZD5/8 was reported to have higher signaling activity and broader Wnt binding and response spectrum.
source: Among them, FZD5/8 was reported to have higher signaling activity and broader Wnt binding and response spectrum (Martin et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from previous literature characterizing FZD5/8 properties.

claim: FZD5 undergoes maturation through specific binding to cholesterol.
source: A recent study suggested that FZD5 undergoes maturation through specific binding to cholesterol (Zheng et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited from recent literature on FZD5 maturation mechanism.

claim: Wnt3a and Wnt5a bind to FZD5/8, FZD4, and FZD7 with similar affinities.
source: Wnt3a and Wnt5a bind to FZD5/8, FZD4, and FZD7 with similar affinities (Li et al., 2023) and specifically induce FZD5/8 but not other FZDs endocytosis.
evidence: Cited from previous binding affinity study.

claim: The Wnt-FZD5/8 complex may recruit another unidentified membrane protein that promotes the internalization of the whole complex.
source: It is possible that the Wnt-FZD5/8 complex recruits another unidentified membrane protein that promotes the internalization of the whole complex.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential mechanism based on study findings.

claim: FZD5, but not the other FZDs, is crucial for the growth of RNF43-mutated pancreatic tumors and colorectal tumor organoids.
source: Our results provide an underlying mechanism for a recent study in which the authors reported that FZD5, but not the other FZDs, is crucial for the growth of RNF43-mutated pancreatic tumors and colorectal tumor organoids (Steinhart et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from previous cancer study, with current study providing mechanistic explanation.

claim: RSPO proteins are present in stem cell niches.
source: RSPO proteins, known as stem cell factors, are present in stem cell niches (de Lau et al., 2011; Yan et al., 2017), while ZNRF3/RNF43 are also expressed in stem cells (Koo et al., 2012; Sato et al., 2011; Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from previous literature on RSPO localization.

claim: ZNRF3/RNF43 are expressed in stem cells.
source: RSPO proteins, known as stem cell factors, are present in stem cell niches (de Lau et al., 2011; Yan et al., 2017), while ZNRF3/RNF43 are also expressed in stem cells (Koo et al., 2012; Sato et al., 2011; Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from previous literature on ZNRF3/RNF43 expression.

claim: FZD5 is expressed in adult stem cells and is essential for their function.
source: FZD5 is expressed in adult stem cells and is essential for their function (Alsaadi et al., 2023; Harada et al., 2021; Nabhan et al., 2023; Yan et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited from multiple previous studies on FZD5 in stem cells.

claim: There are nineteen Wnt ligands and ten Frizzled (FZD) receptors in mammals.
source: There are nineteen Wnt ligands and ten Frizzled (FZD) receptors in mammals (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from established knowledge in the field.

claim: ZNRF3 and RNF43 are closely related transmembrane E3 ubiquitin ligases that are induced by Wnt/β-catenin signaling and antagonize Wnt signaling by promoting FZD receptor endocytosis and degradation.
source: ZNRF3 and RNF43 are closely related transmembrane E3 ubiquitin ligases that are induced by Wnt/β-catenin signaling and antagonize Wnt signaling by promoting FZD receptor endocytosis and degradation (Bugter et al., 2024; Hao et al., 2012; Koo et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from previous literature establishing ZNRF3/RNF43 function.

claim: R-spondin (RSPO) family proteins of stem cell growth factors were reported to potentiate Wnt signaling by binding to and degrading ZNRF3/RNF43 with the help of LGR4 or LGR5.
source: R-spondin (RSPO) family proteins of stem cell growth factors were reported to potentiate Wnt signaling by binding to and degrading ZNRF3/RNF43 with the help of LGR4 or LGR5 (Hao et al., 2012; Kazanskaya et al., 2004; Park et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous literature on RSPO mechanism.

claim: RSPO can activate Wnt signaling through ZNRF3/RNF43 independently of LGRs.
source: However, recent studies have indicated that RSPO can activate Wnt signaling through ZNRF3/RNF43 independently of LGRs (Dubey et al., 2020; Lebensohn and Rohatgi, 2018; Szenker-Ravi et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from recent literature showing LGR-independent RSPO function.

claim: Receptor endocytosis positively influences both the canonical and noncanonical Wnt pathways by facilitating or amplifying intracellular signaling.
source: Numerous studies have reported that receptor endocytosis positively influences both the canonical and noncanonical Wnt pathways by facilitating or amplifying intracellular signaling (Chen et al., 2003; Yamamoto et al., 2006; Yu et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from previous literature on receptor endocytosis in Wnt signaling.

claim: Ligand-induced receptor endocytosis and degradation play critical roles in controlling signal strength and duration and are typical negative regulatory mechanisms in receptor tyrosine kinase pathways.
source: Conversely, ligand-induced receptor endocytosis and degradation play critical roles in controlling signal strength and duration and are typical negative regulatory mechanisms in receptor tyrosine kinase pathways (Alexander, 1998; Haglund and Dikic, 2012; Marmor and Yarden, 2004; Sorkin and Waters, 1993).
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about RTK regulation.

claim: The ubiquitination of intracellular lysine residues serves as a typical sorting signal that can be recognized by the endosomal sorting complexes required for transport (ESCRT) and sorted for lysosomal degradation.
source: The ubiquitination of intracellular lysine residues serves as a typical sorting signal that can be recognized by the endosomal sorting complexes required for transport (ESCRT) and sorted for lysosomal degradation (Cullen and Steinberg, 2018).
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about ubiquitin-mediated sorting.

claim: FZD receptors are classified into four clusters, with sequence variations predominantly in the extracellular CRD domain and C-terminal tail.
source: FZD receptors are classified into four clusters, with sequence variations predominantly in the extracellular CRD domain and C-terminal tail (Huang and Klein, 2004).
evidence: Cited from previous classification study.
